To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) students' spontaneous attributions following success and failure in a math test are dominantly causal and dominantly evaluative, respectively, (2) the causal attributions of students who failed are predominantly internal (i.e., they attribute failure to their own abilities) and the evaluative attributions of students whose performance exceeded their expectations are predominantly positive, and (3) these results are in line with the predictions of Weiner's (1985) model.
students who performed better in a statistics exam tended to report evaluative cognitions and that students who performed worse tended to report causal attributions.

students who performed better in an academic exam than they had expected to do were more likely to report positive feelings and to attribute their success to effort and luck, and students who performed worse than they had expected were more likely to attribute their failure to lack of ability and to report negative feelings.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether spontaneous verbal reports following achievement outcomes are dominated by causal, evaluative or finalistic cognitions.
the question of whether and when spontaneous causal attributions are elicited by success and failure experiences.
the question of what students think and feel after receiving exam results, and with the question of whether these cognitions differ according to the students' success or failure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the study are in line with the hypothesis that the students' causal attributions are influenced by the success or failure they experience.
students who performed better (worse) than they had expected were more likely to attribute the results to themselves (to the task) and to evaluate the performance as good (bad), respectively.
the spontaneous verbal reports following test results are a function of both the students' prior expectations and the actual outcome of the test.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the students who performed better were more likely to produce evaluative thoughts, whereas the ones who performed worse were more inclined to causal reasoning.

students who are uncertain of their performance tend to spontaneously produce causal attributions following failures and evaluative cognitions following successes, whereas students who are certain of their performance do the reverse.
